speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, Southeast Asia is about 680 million people and a US$4 trillion economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And it is young where we are old – median age of Malaysia and Indonesia around 31; Vietnam, 34; the Philippines, 27; against our own citizens' median of nearly 44.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But youth is a window, not a promise.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A demographic window buys a country growth, more workers, not wealth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The region has perhaps 15 to 20 years to get rich before it grows old.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore did climb that ladder by hosting, taking in large amounts of foreign investment to make goods and services for foreign markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The markets everyone leaned on are being weaponised.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A region that produces mainly for markets it does not control can be squeezed at will.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the ground under our own strategy is shifting too.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our hub model carries an assumption: that the gradient between Singapore and its neighbours in competence, in institutions, in trust is permanent.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Penang firms today do nano-level vision inspection that the world's chipmakers buy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For a Singapore whose business model is to be the main place in the region where things work, it is a deadline.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Because a hub, unlike an owner, can be bypassed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Indonesia or Vietnam, at even half their potential, has the demographic weight to become the heart of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And we have to outrun potential resurgent nationalisms that could close doors around us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A Singapore that is merely a well-run waypoint – hosting, brokering, never owning anything together with its neighbours – will find that the region learns, in time, to route around it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we should help build a Southeast Asian market of genuine middle-class consumers – we do not have one at scale today – because a market we help build is far less likely to be closed to us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And we need Singaporeans and Singaporean firms to own a real piece of the value chains that serve it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To be essential to the region and to share in what the region earns.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We must build a deeper, more structural integration with Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Part of what stops us is a posture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In my maiden speech, I asked why Singapore and Malaysia could not build an Airbus together – one enterprise, owned on both sides, the way France and Germany anchored theirs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is not necessarily that our neighbours cannot execute.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Penang's equipment firms and Selangor's chip designers put that to rest.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The real reasons are older: memories of past issues, from water to the railway lands; a reflex to keep control of anything that matters; and a fear of bets stranded across a border if politics turn.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But if one is sceptical that the gradient between Singapore and our neighbours will last – and I am – then joint industrial policy is what a country should build while the gradient still favours it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe the strongest path to owning things together runs through our closest neighbour, Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Malaysia's industrial strategy now deliberately targets the design end of semiconductors, setting up the region's first IC-design park in Selangor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The integration is happening anyway – by drift.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two hundred and forty-five million checkpoint crossings last year, three-quarters of them by land.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we get them right, we can prove a model of structural bilateral integration that we can extend.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This economic zone lets two governments run inside the bounded space and experiment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The zone has been a blank slate many have piled their hopes onto.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some ideas put to me were high-tech food-growing zones, an ASEAN Friendship Hospital in Johor, an integrated medical hub on the Shenzhen-Hong Kong model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But hopes need us to bring the zone into greater focus.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Nine flagship areas have been announced, described at the level of districts; I have not seen a consolidated boundary map.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, what does a Singapore company receive inside the JS-SEZ, over and above the new federal baseline?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Malaysia's New Incentive Framework took effect for manufacturing on 1 March.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the federal incentives are as good as the zone's, there is nothing special about the zone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, I believe we should soon sort out, with our Malaysian counterparts, one standard operating procedure to enter the zone and one rulebook.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Right now, there are multiple agencies and points of contact.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On the Malaysian side, there is the Iskandar Regional Development Authority, Invest Johor, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) and the Invest Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On the Singapore side, we have the Economic Development Board (EDB) one-stop centre.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need policy clarity and joint rules of the road over how companies can enter the zone, whether from Malaysia or Singapore, so that the private sector can plan for it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: With a joint rulebook, we should measure joint success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In my view that means EDB or the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) should be responsible for total key performance indicators (KPIs) over the JS-SEZ, not just the Singapore-originated investments alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Of course, a large degree of self-interested thinking is inevitable and even desirable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The instinct in parts of our Government may be to keep the high-value activity here and let the rest go.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But if we want the unfolding of a richer, more complex, more diverse value chain within a 60-kilometre radius than would currently be possible in 10 or 20 years, we will need to take a more collaborative approach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe we should grade ourselves, EDB and the Ministry on the SEZ's success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the zone is meant to be more than just a new method of foreign direct investment, but to foster a vibrant set of Singaporean and Malaysian businesses, in pursuit of broadening the middle class, does it actually build on the current set of bilateral strengths?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The foremost candidate for such an industrial deepening is semiconductors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But here, using the instrument of the zone may be an impedance mismatch, as in my view Penang's semiconductor cluster is unlikely to relocate beyond the Klang Valley.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we will need a broader set of instruments.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What can we hope for from semiconductors as joint industrial policy?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our IC-design strength is mostly the design centres of foreign firms on our soil.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have not grown a chip-design champion of our own, and we sold our indigenous foundry, Chartered Semiconductor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, Malaysia is building some of what we lack.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Selangor's IC-design park, the largest in Southeast Asia, turns out hundreds of designers a year; the Penang design house whose listing I described came out of this push; and Singapore's own state-linked capital is already backing Malaysian design start-ups.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have more reason to complement each other than to compete.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Singapore hosts what the region's designers require: wafer fabs to prototype on, advanced packaging, capital and customers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They hold some of what we require: design talent, by the hundreds, at a fraction of our cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Neither side has a complete owned upstream stack alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Since we sold Chartered, we have no fabs of our own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, first, we should allow Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) funds to lease or rent Singapore-based fab lines so that we can put real silicon in front of the region's designers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: While those fabs are still under construction, we should supplement investments to expand directable fab capacity where possible, prioritising Singapore businesses but open to Malaysian ones as well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This, I think, is the best way to validate the viability of a chip design ecosystem while giving it the best chance of success – iterative prototyping feedback inside the same regional corridor, especially if one is understandably hesitant for a full-scale US$15 to US$20-billion two-nanometre fab rebuild.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When people from both countries own part of the same success, each has reason to grow its own capability rather than to poach it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should seek to create rails that work for a recognised category of bilateral joint firms across the two countries, and crowd in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, in service of crowding in, we should reactivate the Malaysia-Singapore Business Development Fund.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It was set up in 2004 for exactly this, enhanced in 2023, relaunched in 2024.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: As far as I know, it has not been used.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, we should give it a fresh purpose: competitive seed awards into the first recognised Malaysia-Singapore ventures – many small bets, fast answers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Integration will arrive as a train in 2027, up to 10,000 passengers an hour each way.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Walk our heartland shops today and you can feel the dread coming.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Eleven million Singaporean trips into Johor in the first seven months of last year alone validate this.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government's answer so far is to make retail more attractive at home – visual-merchandising programmes, placemaking grants, neighbourhood centre upgrades, vouchers to spend at home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But we should be honest with ourselves: for a generation of retailers, it will make little difference.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe we can offer a different deal.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Johor is planning the Elevated Autonomous Rapid Transit (e-ART) system as a dispersal network out of Bukit Chagar, and I speculate that transit-oriented development will be done in the vicinity of their 32 stations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If so, I propose we invest in that plan: as part of the JS-SEZ bargain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When Singapore and Malaysia resolved, in 2010, the 20-year impasse over the 1990 Points of Agreement on the railway lands, it was not settled in cash but in co-ownership.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It should go to the tenant and not the owner of the unit since the renter carries lost footfall with nothing to fall back on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Retail is a more protected part of Malaysia's economy, so the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and MTI would need to negotiate this within the same bargain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Since Malaysia has already carved foreign firms into Forest City, it is not unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We can seek this compact if it is possible, for our small retailers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is a better deal than the fait accompli they currently await.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, in closing, I do not pretend any of this is inevitable or easy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Foreign economic relations are always challenging, with reduced control and increased unpredictability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But we are in a unique moment, where the threat and leverage of market closure from the biggest powers are foremost on our minds.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And we are also reaching the limits of our growth on 750 square kilometres.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It would be a shame if the JS-SEZ and the tenor of our future cooperation with Malaysia were predominantly foreign direct investments-led, instead of being in service of tackling the true strategic challenges of the decade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The creation of a true middle class in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An integration of our country, to be indispensable to the future economic geometries of our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An imperative to increase the complexity and diversity of our value chains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And how do we ensure that integration does not simply move activity from Singapore to somewhere else, but also creates value in Singapore and our partners which would otherwise not be captured?

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singapore has always been open to the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I think, in the transport Motion, many of you have already said that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And with investment competition intensifying and supply chains reconfiguring, we must keep building our capabilities, strengthening our businesses and anchoring higher-value activities here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The JS-SEZ, the Batam-Bintan-Karimun region and the Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Parks are all examples that show how we work with our immediate neighbours to enlarge economic space for our companies and workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This was something that the Member Edward Chia had said earlier on in his speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singapore has strong connectivity, trusted institutions, deep financing, technology, professional services, headquarters (HQ) functions and a skilled workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Johor, on the other hand, offers land production capacity and other complementary strengths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But when we combine these strengths well, the Johor-Singapore region becomes more competitive than either side would be on its own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Member talked about whether there being so many different touch points, but in fact, if you look at it on the Malaysia side, there is, as he mentioned, the IMFC-J, which facilitates and supports companies investing in the zone, such as coordinating approvals and applications across Malaysian authorities at the federal, state and local levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In Singapore, we also have a joint JS-SEZ Project Office, which helps Singapore and Singapore-based companies explore twinning opportunities in the JS-SEZ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have gone to many of these workshops and both offices work hand-in-hand together to facilitate investments coming through to Johor, to the zone; and from Singapore to the zone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The refreshed Johor-Singapore Cooperation Ministerial Committee, co-chaired by Minister Chee Hong Tat and Malaysian Minister for Economy Akmal Nasrullah, will also provide strategic oversight for broader cooperation including the SEZ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On the reason why we are pursuing this and how this is a core strategy in integrating with the region, the JS-SEZ is all about tapping our complementary strengths for a win-win outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The JS-SEZ is focused on the Johor-Singapore corridor and building on the respective incentives and schemes offered by each country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Both countries are working on introducing practical solutions like smoother cross-border flow of goods and people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I understand the concerns also that deeper integration could move activities out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But I think as the Member alluded to, we cannot also accommodate every activity within Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Instead, our approach has and always been to keep Singapore as a key node while helping our companies scale and build resilience so that we can compete globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This means organising practical and meaningful activities across both sides of the Causeway, so we can continue to play to our strengths as a financial, transportation and tech hub, and also to anchor HQ functions, R&D, intellectual property, talent development and other high value activities here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Old Chang Kee, which is a food manufacturer in Singapore, has operated a production facility in Gelang Patah since 2016, complementing its Singapore operations and supporting its retail outlets in both markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: South Korea's SPC Group, the parent company of Paris Baguette and Shake Shack, houses its Southeast Asia HQ, innovation centre and training centres in Singapore, while operating its production base in Johor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And then we move into semiconductors which the Member had talked about quite significantly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And we will keep strengthening Singapore's position as a key node in this global semiconductor value chain by attracting quality investments and anchoring higher-value activities here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our strategy is not to replicate what is being done in Johor or Penang, but to work with Malaysia on complementary activities that strengthen the regional ecosystem for semiconductors, which is a very fast and evolving sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Another example here to illustrate this point is STMicroelectronics which anchored its Asia Pacific HQ and wafer fab operations in Singapore, complemented by assembly and test operations, including high reliability automotive packaging in Johor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Their wafers fabricated in Singapore directly feed into packaging and qualification in Malaysia, enabling STMicroelectronics to bring products to market faster.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Member also talked about how we measure these investments or what are the KPIs for the JS-SEZ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Well, the JS-SEZ must deliver real investments, business activity and jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It has so far garnered significant and strong business interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we are not just focused on the headline investment numbers but whether the JS-SEZ expands the overall pie for the region and for Singapore and Johor together competing for investments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On the RTS Link, I chair the RTS Link Taskforce to help Singaporeans and businesses benefit from the RTS Link.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have been widely engaging residents, merchants, trade associations, landlords and other stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Based on the feedback we have received, we are working on measures to further rejuvenate our heartlands, help our businesses become more competitive, transform, pivot and work with the private sector to promote business and commerce on both sides.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Some of the work has already begun on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have spoken to the private sector players on both sides.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But I think we should be clear about the broader point.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The way to respond to greater connectivity is not to retreat from competition, as the Member had alluded to; but to help our businesses to compete more effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Competition does not just come across from the Causeway.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Already, it comes from digital platforms, international brands, AI-enabled services, e-commerce and changing consumer preferences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On his suggestions about different deals with the Malaysians, I think it is within their jurisdiction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I think we do what we can under the auspices of the JS-SEZ to ensure that our companies can invest there confidently and also anchor strong and high value activities here, complementing both Singapore and Malaysia, Singapore and Johor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The test is not whether every activity must be located here – of course, that would be unrealistic with our constraints – but whether Singapore remains where the highest value functions are anchored, where important decisions are made, where we can build capabilities and where we ultimately can create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And if a company does choose the Johor-Singapore region instead of another location elsewhere in Asia and anchors its HQ functions, financing, innovation and R&D activities in Singapore, then I think that is additive integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And if our companies can use Johor as a complementary base to scale, serve larger markets and strengthen their regional competitiveness while retaining their core capabilities here, that is also additive integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And if our region as a whole becomes more attractive to global investors and Singapore captures the higher-value parts of that value chain, that is also additive integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is the approach, Mr Speaker, that we are taking to ensure that regional integration benefits Singapore and Singaporeans.
